targets.note: the person's question is how occupancy, residence times and transition rates change as the stiffness ratio goes from 1 to 100, which is a question about trends over two decades. One decade of resolution on each is enough to answer it, and the prototype already shows the occupancy law is sharper than that. well_occupancy is named as the observable because the goal card carries one; well_residence_time, interwell_transition_rate and interwell_barrier_height are measured from the same trajectory and belong to the same question

constraint_notes: THE MODEL IS THE PERSON'S, 2026-09-23: U1 = 1/2 kt (x-a1)^2 and U2 = 1/2 a kt (x-a2)^2, with the separation a2-a1 held FIXED and only the stiffness ratio a varied from 1 to 100. The person withdrew an earlier proposal to set the separation to a/2

the two wells are combined as the LOWER of the two, U = min(U1, U2). Their SUM has no barrier at any separation or ratio -- the curvature is kt(1+a) everywhere and the separation cancels -- so the sum cannot answer the question. min is a modelling convention and not optics, and that is stated rather than assumed silently

no configuration in contracts/capabilities/simulation.json declares this model, so S3.0 screening refuses all four observables today and this card stays DRAFT: it cannot proceed to S3 until the configuration is declared, which is a write to contracts/ and not this agent's
one dimension, along the axis joining the traps. The transverse directions are not integrated

numbers.name: temperature
numbers.note: the room's, not established to be the sample's

numbers.name: diffusivity
numbers.note: the store's relation (kb:tracer_diffusivity_expected), not a second copy

numbers.name: trap_separation
numbers.note: held fixed across the whole sweep, as the person specified. The separation sets the timescale of the answer and not the answer: the occupancy ratio comes out the same at every separation tried

numbers.name: barrier_at_ratio_one
numbers.note: low enough that hopping is fast at ratio 1, and because the barrier's whole stiffness dependence is a/(1+sqrt(a))^2, which saturates at four times its ratio-1 value, it can rise only to 6.6 kT at ratio 100, where both directions still hop inside a run

numbers.name: trap_stiffness_soft
numbers.note: the soft trap's stiffness that puts the ratio-1 barrier where the window says. Inherits the assumed separation's grade. Well below a normal trapping stiffness, which is what thermal hopping requires

assumptions.statement: One micrometre is a separation two traps steered by the instrument's deflector can be set to, and it is comparable to the particle size in a way that keeps the picture of one particle between two foci meaningful. Nothing measured picks it.
assumptions.falsifier: a separation read back from the particle's own position histogram replaces it; a commanded value does not, because the instrument has no readback

assumptions.statement: The range 1 to 100 is the person's, given in the question.
A 2 kT barrier at ratio 1 keeps every ratio up to 100 inside a barrier window where both wells are visited within one run.
assumptions.falsifier: an A2 interval showing the ratio-100 dwell cannot be sampled inside budget at this barrier replaces it

kb_refs.claim: The particles in the bottle in use have a diameter of 5 micrometres, with a coefficient of variation no greater than 2 per cent, measured directly by the operator on 2026-09-19.

The laboratory's ambient temperature is 20 degrees Celsius, read off a thermometer by the operator. It is a reading and not a setpoint, and it is the room's rather than the sample's -- which is what makes it an operator reading at E3 and not a calibration at E2.
Dynamic viscosity of pure water near 293 K is of order one millipascal second, and it changes by roughly two percent per kelvin in that neighbourhood.

The expected translational diffusivity of a tracer sphere in a bulk fluid is the Stokes-Einstein value, k_B T over 3 pi eta d. It is a prediction from the viscosity, the temperature and the diameter, not a measurement of how the particles actually move.
